approach: Secondary analysis of the BR.34 trial. Patients were classified into AM group (≥80% infusions before 13:00) or PM group based on prior literature thresholds. OS and PFS were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for imbalanced baseline factors. Sensitivity analyses tested alternative TOI thresholds (≥60% before 13:00; median TOI 11:00). Safety profiles were compared between groups.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides empirical evidence that afternoon infusion of dual ICI (durvalumab-tremelimumab) is associated with superior survival outcomes compared to morning infusion in advanced NSCLC, contrasting with earlier reports on anti-PD-1 monotherapy.
contribution_and_limits.limits: Based on secondary analysis of a single trial (BR.34); observational nature limits causal inference regarding circadian mechanisms; generalizability to other tumor types or ICI combinations requires prospective validation as noted by authors.

key_findings.conditions: Overall cohort (296 evaluable patients: 186 AM, 110 PM)
key_findings.finding: PM infusion associated with longer median OS (19.1 vs 13.4 months; HR 0.58) and PFS (8.3 vs 4.1 months; HR 0.67).
PM administration remained significantly associated with improved OS (aHR 0.62) and PFS (aHR 0.73).
Consistent trends favoring later infusions for OS/PFS across both treatment arms.
No apparent difference in fatal adverse events or serious adverse effects leading to discontinuation between AM and PM groups.

problem_or_question: To assess whether the timing of drug administration (morning vs. afternoon) affects overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) in patients receiving dual ICI therapy, given emerging evidence for anti-PD-1 monotherapy but limited data for dual checkpoint blockade.
research_scope: Advanced EGFR/ALK-negative non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients treated with durvalumab-tremelimumab ± platinum chemotherapy in the CCTG BR34 trial context.
work_summary: This study investigates whether the time of infusion (TOI) of dual immune checkpoint inhibitors correlates with clinical outcomes, addressing the limited evidence on circadian biology's impact on dual blockade efficacy. It is a secondary analysis of the BR.34 trial data.
